column8: The armies and the ground. Middleton counted 886 men on land: militia from Winnipeg, Toronto and Ontario towns, mounted scouts, and gunners of A Battery. He had four nine-pounder guns, a Gatling gun, and about fifty more men on the steamer. The defenders were May-tee, Cree and Dakota fighters, perhaps 250 to 300 at the start. Their numbers changed as the battle went on. They had hunting rifles, shotguns and old muzzle-loaders, and little ammunition. The village lay on the east bank of the river. To the south, the church and the rectory stood on higher ground, with the cemetery beyond. Along the wooded slopes and ravines, the defenders had dug rifle pits: holes three or four feet deep with a low wall of earth and logs, hard to see and hard to hit.

In the pits, cartridges are running out. Witnesses describe men searching the ground the soldiers have left for dropped cartridges, and melting down lead. Hildebrandt writes that some fired nails when the bullets made from scavenged lead ran out, and Bishop Grandin later said they were reduced to firing small stones and nails. How often that happened is uncertain.

The army won. Hildebrandt counts twenty-five dead in the four days: soldiers, May-tee and First Nations. By the last day, only 50 to 60 defenders were still fighting, with about 40 rifles between them; the rest had double-barrelled shotguns. Middleton walked over the ground afterwards. He wrote that he was "astonished at the strength of the position and at the ingenuity and care displayed in the construction of the rifle pits." On the last day Ree-el had written on the back of one of Middleton's messages: "I do not like war." On the 13th of May Middleton wrote that he would receive Ree-el and his council and protect them until the government decided their case. Ree-el answered: "My council are dispersed. I wish you would let them go quiet and free… I will go to fulfil God's will." On the 15th of May he gave himself up to two scouts. Gabriel Doo-mon refused to surrender. "I still have ninety cartridges to spend on his men," he answered. He stayed near Ba-tosh for some days, then escaped to the United States. Poundmaker came in to Battleford on the 26th of May, and Big Bear gave himself up at Fort Carlton on the 2nd of July. Both were sent to prison, and both died soon after their release in 1887. Ree-el was tried for high treason at Regina, before a jury of six English-speaking men. His lawyers argued that he was insane; Ree-el himself rejected that defence in his speeches to the jury. The jury found him guilty but asked for mercy. He was hanged on the 16th of November 1885. Eleven days later, on the 27th of November, six Cree and two Nakoda (Assiniboine) men were hanged together at Battleford. Ree-el's death divided Canada for a generation, French against English, Catholic against Protestant. For the May-tee of Ba-tosh, the war's end brought loss. Many homes had been burned or looted. Some sold the land scrip they were given for far less than it was worth, and many moved away, north and west. Doo-mon later toured the United States with Buffalo Bill's Wild West show. After an amnesty he came home, and he died near Ba-tosh in 1906. Today Ba-tosh is a National Historic Site. Ree-el, once hanged as a traitor, is remembered as the founder of Manitoba, and statues of Ree-el and Doo-mon stand in Winnipeg and Saskatoon.
